paragraphs: Spring came later to the lands north of the Huai than to Jiangnan. As the last days of the second month slipped away, last year’s dead reeds still covered the river flats. When the wind passed, their leaves scraped against one another with a dry, rasping sound. Government men had driven slender stakes into the ground along the levee, each marked in vermilion with a measure of acreage, one every few paces. The newcomers from the south followed the line of stakes. Some tested the soil with the toes of their shoes; others crouched to take a handful of earth, smell it, and let it fall.

Chen Shuo stood at the edge of the flats looking over the plot allotted to him. It lay low, its soil was sandy, and beyond it ran a deep gully gouged out by last year’s flood. His wife, Ahe, asked, “When the heavy rains come, whose fields will flood first?”
“Ours,” Chen Shuo said.

Ahe held their daughter, Chen Man, in her arms. She glanced at her husband without complaint. She only wanted to know how they would repay the seed borrowed from the government after the autumn harvest. The junior official in charge of the fields was already surrounded by so many petitioners that his belt was nearly being pulled loose. One family wanted to know whether they could stay after three years. Another asked who would pay if a borrowed ox fell and died. An elderly woman kept demanding to know whether a trip back to Jiangnan to tend her husband’s grave during those three years would count as absconding from the register.

The official turned through his documents for half the day, sweat gathering on his brow. Xue Zhi was riding along the levee when he heard someone shout, “The government said it would give us land, but not how we’re to live by farming it!” He reined in and ordered every question written down; any that could not be answered that day would receive a posted reply within three days. The crowd did not disperse. Instead several households pressed up to his horse and raised their old grain-debt contracts. Xue Zhi had seen armies in disorder on the battlefield, but he found these dozens of damp sheets harder to confront than spears.

Shen Lingyi had not come to contend for land. She had been given an abandoned granary at the eastern end of the guest settlement. The beams were still sound, though wind entered at the corners, and last year’s spoiled reed mats lay piled inside. Xue Zhi had authorized her to open a school and allotted three years of grain rations. The Secretariat’s orders said nothing so particular as where books, desks, or charcoal for the winter were to come from. So she and her seventeen pupils first carried away the mildewed mats, then nailed long tables together from scraps of timber. Zhou Shu’s urn stood beneath a roof beam, his old official robes folded neatly beside it. Each day as she swept, she avoided that place, as though her husband might still object to dust settling on his books.

For the first two days, only children from the south attended. People peered in over the outer wall and asked whether local children would have to pay a teacher’s fee. Shen Lingyi said they would not. One man laughed: southerners were drawing government rations, he said, and now meant to steal the northerners' livelihood in teaching as well. On the third day, Feng Shun brought his grandson Feng Qi by the hand. He scolded the boy the whole way for refusing to wash his face, but at the doorway the old man faltered, several times nearly turning back with him.

“His father died repairing the levee,” Feng Shun said at last. “The land the county promised our family is still half a mu short, even now. When I’m dead, who will know how to claim what those deeds say is his?”
Feng Qi looked down, tugging at the hem of his clothes. Suddenly he asked Shen Lingyi, “If I learn to read, will the county give our land back?”
Shen Lingyi brought out a board she had wiped clean. “Perhaps not. But when they hand you a paper next time, you will be able to read it for yourself.”

Feng Shun pushed his grandson inside. Before leaving he told her she could slap the boy’s palm if he misbehaved. Shen Lingyi said she did not strike children. The old man snorted, but when he reached the levee he turned and gazed through the doorway for a long time. At noon that day, Feng Qi and Chen Man quarreled over a brush and began cursing in the accents of their respective homes. Shen Lingyi caught a few of the words, took the brush away, and made them write their names in turns. The southern children saw that Feng Qi had written the character for seven so crookedly that it looked like a sickle, and doubled over laughing at their desks. His face burned. He rubbed it out and wrote it again, refusing to leave until dusk had entered the windows.

On the ninth day of the third month, a large boat bearing the crest of the Lu family arrived at the ferry. Seventy-three people were aboard. Those belowdecks sat packed together, and several women near the hatch had their clothes soaked through. As soon as the vessel touched shore, more than ten guards carrying staves disembarked. They were followed by a man whose robes and headwear were impeccably arranged.

He introduced himself to commandant Li Qian as Lu Chang of Wu Commandery, handed over eight short blades and three bows, and even produced a list giving the age and native place of everyone aboard. Li Qian thought he had met someone who would make his work easy. But at the end of the list he frowned. More than twenty tenant dependents had no separate household names; all were entered together as “members of the Lu household.”
“These entries must be separated,” Li Qian said, pushing the register back.

Lu Chang glanced at his servants, still unloading baggage on the bank, and his expression cooled. “They have lived on the Lu estate for generations and crossed with us in time of trouble. The respective stations of landowner and tenant have long been established. Why manufacture difficulties?”

The registration clerk replied, “If someone aboard falls ill, or owes money, or is separated from the rest of the family, we must know who that person is. The words 'Lu household' will not help us find a missing man.”

Lu Chang did not argue at once. He ordered his steward, Lu Qing, to present the chest of contracts. Inside, land deeds, grain-loan accounts, and tenancy agreements were bundled by year with a meticulousness almost worthy of admiration. The clerk had barely opened the first roll when a weather-beaten man stepped forward. In a low voice he said his name was Chen Shuo, formerly of Wucheng; his wife was Ahe and his daughter Chen Man. He requested to be registered as a household in his own right.

Lu Qing seized him by the collar. Li Qian caught the steward’s hand and made him let go. Chen Shuo did not retreat. His legs trembled, but he spoke distinctly. “I’ll pay the Lu family’s boat fare. I acknowledge the grain lent to my father, too. But if the government gives out land from now on, I want to farm it with Ahe ourselves.”

Lu Chang’s face changed. He remembered Chen Shuo’s father coming in a year of flood, sick and struggling, to borrow twenty shi of grain. He remembered how the Lu family had engaged a physician for Chen Shuo and paid his service levy, and even that he himself had sent a bolt of cloth for Chen Shuo’s wedding. Everyone had been grateful for such acts in those days. Now, on the other side of the river, it was as though an old sheet of paper had been lifted to reveal what lay underneath.
“Your father entrusted you to me on his deathbed,” Lu Chang said.
Chen Shuo looked at the Huai, running like the river he had left in the south. “He entrusted you with my care. He didn’t sell me to you.”

Xue Zhi did not dare decide the case alone. In the command tent, they opened the chest of accounts. Fifteen years of entries crowded the pages, down to a wagon axle or half a bolt of hemp cloth, and together they came to a debt reckoned at 137 shi of grain. The rent Chen Shuo’s family had paid and the days they had spent repairing canals and standing night watch were entered in another ledger, never credited against the debt. Rent was rent and labor service was service, Lu Qing maintained; how could either be confused with borrowed grain? Lu Chang had his reasons as well. If great households opened their granaries in a famine and fortified their estates when marauders came, only to see everyone leave once their lives were saved, who would ever dare bear such risks for the poor again?

Xue Zhi did not dismiss his argument. After years guarding the Huai, he knew government granaries sometimes opened too late, and some villages had survived raiding cavalry only because of a great clan’s fortified compound. Yet the twenty shi Chen Shuo’s father had borrowed had multiplied severalfold in little more than a decade, while the labor of three family members counted for nothing against it. Xue Zhi asked Lu Qing whether Chen Man would be free to leave if Chen Shuo died tomorrow. With the debt unpaid, Lu Qing answered, the daughter would naturally remain a tenant dependent.

Feng Shun had been listening behind the tent for half the day. Now he struck his walking stick against the ground. As a young man, he said, he too had borrowed an ox. When the animal died, he had owed another ox; unable to repay at once, he had paid by degrees. But the landowner had never come to ask how many shi of grain his grandson was worth. Lu Qing was about to flare up. Lu Chang raised a hand to stop him.

Xue Zhi issued a provisional ruling. Chen Shuo’s family would be registered separately as a guest household. County clerks and independent witnesses from outside the Lu estate would examine the old debt entry by entry. The Lu family was forbidden to seize anyone privately; until the inquiry ended, the Chen family must remain in its settlement, so neither side could allege that the others had fled. Lu Chang said he would petition the court in Chang’an. Xue Zhi permitted him to go and sealed the case papers.

That night fire broke out in the guest settlement. Feng Qi was first to see the flames. He ran barefoot, crying out for Teacher Shen to save them. Shen Lingyi rushed to the thatched shelters, where smoke filled everything before her eyes. Chen Man was huddled beneath her mother’s body at the foot of an earthen wall, blood running from her forehead. Several household guards brought by Lu Qing were still trying to carry off the Chen family’s chests; there was blood on their cudgels, and Chen Shuo had been beaten so badly he could not lift his hands. Feng Shun arrived with an axe for chopping firewood and smashed Lu Qing’s shoulder with its blunt back, only to be thrown down himself and have two ribs broken. By the time patrolling soldiers separated them, half the shelter had burned. By good fortune, no one had been killed.

Lu Chang arrived only at daybreak. Standing beneath a charred post, he saw Chen Man clutching a pair of straw sandals scorched by the fire, and for a moment he could hardly recognize in what had happened the Lu family he thought he knew. He did not interfere when Lu Qing was punished. Yet he would still go to Chang’an and demand a ruling on whether old contracts remained binding across the Huai. Before he left, he apologized to Chen Shuo. Chen Shuo asked just one question: “Lord Lu, if old Feng hadn’t come last night, would my daughter already be serving the old lady of your house?” Lu Chang could not answer.

The party bound for the capital followed the Ru and Ying rivers north. Lu Chang rode on horseback; Chen Shuo sat on the ox cart carrying the case papers. They seldom spoke by daylight. At an inn, Lu Chang sent medicine for Chen Shuo’s wounds, and the next morning the bottle was returned unopened. He asked Chen Shuo directly whether he refused to acknowledge even that much of their old affection. Chen Shuo shook his head. He was afraid, he said, that the medicine would also be entered in the account book.

Lu Chang was furious on the spot, but thereafter he gave no further orders to keep accounts. Passing Xuchang, they fell into conversation with a post-station clerk about the local land allocations. The imperial order was clear, the clerk said, but in practice some still concealed their good land and declared their barren fields instead. County officers had to investigate year after year. If the change could not be carried out, Lu Chang asked, why make it at all? The clerk was feeding the animals. Without looking up he replied, “If no one investigates, we won’t even know whose hands the wrongdoing passed through.”

The hearing in Chang’an was held at the academy in the southern suburbs. More people came to listen than the officials had expected. Northern landowners attended alongside scholars from the south. Those who had lent grain feared the government would repudiate their debts; those who had borrowed feared being placed once more on their former masters' household rolls. Lu Chang spoke lucidly of fortified estates protecting villagers, providing for their dependents, and paying levies on their behalf. Not a few listeners nodded. He made no claim to have acted without self-interest: he admitted that the Lu estate had received land and labor in return for its grain loans. What he feared was that the state could free old dependents but could not stand in place of their former masters when the next winter famine came.

When Chen Shuo’s turn came, he held out hands not yet healed. He had no polished petition, only a creased sheet bearing his guest-household registration, which he placed on the table. Crown Prince Fu Hong asked whether he was willing to repay the borrowed grain. Yes, he said. Would he acknowledge the passage fare as well? Yes again. Why, then, would he not stay with the Lu family? A long time passed before he answered. He had farmed for fifteen years. His greatest fear was not failing to pay his debts. It was that by the time his daughter grew up, she would already be recorded as someone’s tenant dependent without even knowing to whom she owed anything.

Shen Lingyi testified next. Some elderly people in the settlement, she said, had asked of their own accord to remain with the Lu family, while some women feared farming independently. A single written order could not choose how people ought to live. She spoke of Chen Man, whose burns had not healed, still carrying her schoolbag. Lu Chang finally looked up at the little girl sitting far away. When Chen Man saw his gaze turn to her, she quietly hid behind Feng Qi. A muscle moved in Lu Chang’s face.

Yuan Ji, an envoy of the Jin court, also attended. He bore an official dispatch from Jiankang, requesting that Qin return Jin subjects who had fled compulsory service or left the dependents of private households. The hearing grew tense. Fu Jian came to listen for half the day, but would not allow it to become a debate over which dynasty was legitimate. He ordered the household office first to register military households that had deserted, people implicated in homicide, private debts, and those wishing to return as distinct cases. An entire boatload of people could not be sent back merely on the strength of an official document from Jin.

Yuan Ji asked what would become of the old contracts. Fu Hong presented several audited account books. A documented grain loan could be acknowledged, he said, but no debt contract entitled a private individual to detain another person. Yuan Ji protested that this was an attempt to seize Jin subjects. Fu Jian told him to summon Chen Man and ask the child, face to face, whether she wished to return to Jiangnan and work off her debt to the Lu household. Looking at her, Yuan Ji fell silent for a moment. In the end he stood by his mission’s instructions and demanded that his objections be sent back to Jiankang.

The review continued another seven days. The Lu family’s accounts were checked against years of Chen family rent, labor service, medical bills, and passage fares. The original 137-shi debt was reduced to twenty-nine. The unlawful seizure case from Xue Zhi’s earlier hearing was judged separately: Lu Qing was to be punished for assault, arson, and private detention. The Lu family’s willingness to acknowledge the accounting could not wipe those offenses away.

The court permitted repayment of legitimate grain debts by installments, but prohibited pledging children as security. Tenants willing to remain with the Lu household could sign contracts for fixed terms under official witness. Loans of land and draft animals would be accounted for separately; an old agreement could not bind descendants to hereditary dependence. The edict did not presume to guarantee that these measures would work in every county.

Lu Chang read the judgment but did not leave. He asked Fu Hong, “If there is another famine in the north next year and the government cannot distribute grain, on whom will the people who leave me depend?”
“First we must know where they live and how much grain they lack,” Fu Hong said. “If we cannot provide it, we must report that truthfully and leave them a way to petition.”
“When the Lu estate opens its granaries, at least we do not wait for three documents to be approved first.”
“Which is why the court does not forbid you to open them. But you cannot lock people inside the granary in return.”

Lu Chang lowered his eyes for a long while, then folded the ruling into his sleeve. In the end he returned to the lands north of the Huai. He sought no office and did not go back to Jin. The seventy-three people were divided into nineteen households. Some of the old Lu tenants went their own way; others chose to sign new five-year agreements. Before the elders pressed their thumbprints onto the papers, they asked Shen Lingyi to read them aloud three times. Lu Chang stood beside them. When she came to the clause, “Upon expiry, they may freely choose to stay or depart,” he said nothing more.

Chen Shuo received seven mu of sandy farmland. Before he could sow it, he had to clear the drainage ditch. Feng Shun’s ribs still hurt, but he brought over his old ox and announced that the loan for a season would cost two dou of grain, not half a sheng less. Did he want a written receipt, Chen Shuo asked. Feng Shun glared and told him to bring the grain to his doorstep after harvest and not try any tricks. They argued about which side of the field bank should receive water first, more fiercely than they had argued about last year’s contracts. By midday, though, Feng Shun handed him a pot of hot water and urged him not to faint under the sun.

More northern children joined Shen Lingyi’s school, along with several adults who could not read but listened through the window. As Chen Man learned to write the character *Man* in her own name, she kept leaving out a horizontal stroke. She asked her teacher whether her registration paper would become worthless if they still had nowhere to go after three years. Shen Lingyi offered no easy assurance. She made the girl finish writing her name carefully. Then she took up her brush and, beside the guest-household register, recorded the wound Chen Man had suffered in that year’s fire, lest someone later claim the incident had never happened.

The following day two newly arrived children asked Chen Man whether the northerners got first choice of brushes at the school, leaving the southerners to take what remained. Chen Man hesitated, then offered them the worn bamboo-handled brush she had been using and told them both to begin with the first horizontal stroke. Feng Qi laughed at how she used to leave strokes out, until a glare from her silenced him. A little later all three were crowded around the long table, their sleeves stained from the same dish of ink.

As summer approached, a man came to the ferry carrying an old marriage certificate dated “the nineteenth year of Taiyuan of the Great Jin.” A Qin clerk wanted to enter the date under the Qin calendar. The man clutched the document and would not release it, afraid that changing the words would erase the marriage his father had presided over and the home they had left in Jiangnan. The dispute reached Chang’an. In the end, the Secretariat ordered only that a note of verification be added; the old writing was not to be altered.

When the man came back, he saw his original Jin date beside its corresponding Qin entry in the register. He said nothing for a long time. The clerk assumed he would argue over whose reign title counted. Instead, the man tucked the marriage certificate inside his robe and said softly, “This will do. The old people at home will still recognize it.”
